title: Video Scene Segmentation with Genre and Duration Signals
claim: Injecting precomputed semantic priors into an encoder and sampling training anchors by a simple statistic yields better self-supervised representations.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right, three shaded modules with a genre database below
description: A wide left-to-right pipeline diagram. On the far left, a dashed box holds a shot sequence of movie frames. These feed a pink shaded Shot Encoder block: Self Attention, then Affinity Mapping (highlighted in red), then a Projection Matrix, joined by a multiply node and a residual plus node. Below, a Genre Prompt (for example a Sci-Fi definition in green and red text) passes through a Text Encoder into a cylinder database of precomputed genre embeddings (Drama, Comedy, Horror and others). Arrows from the cylinder condition the Affinity Mapping and Projection Matrix. The encoder output is a Representation Sequence of frames. On the far right, a Pseudo Boundary Generation panel shows a column of shot durations in frames. Short shots are picked as sampled anchors, with a red arrow marking the boundary search space.
caption: Our framework integrates genre embeddings into the shot encoder via affinity-based residual connections and uses duration-aware anchor sampling to generate pseudo-boundaries for selfsupervised shot representation learning in scene segmentation.
abstract: Video scene segmentation aims to detect semantically coherent boundaries in long-form videos, bridging the gap between low-level visual signals and high-level narrative understanding. However, existing methods primarily rely on visual similarity between adjacent shots, which makes it difficult to accurately identify scene boundaries, especially when semantic transitions do not align with visual changes. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that incorporates production-level metadata, specifically genre conventions and shot duration patterns, into video scene segmentation. Our main contributions are three-fold: (1) we leverage textual genre definitions as semantic priors to guide shot-level representation learning during self-supervised pretraining, enabling better capture of narrative coherence; (2) we introduce a duration-aware anchor selection strategy that prioritizes shorter shots based on empirical duration statistics, improving pseudo-boundary generation quality; (3) we propose a test-time shot splitting strategy that subdivides long shots into segments for improved temporal modeling. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on MovieNet-SSeg and BBC datasets. We introduce MovieChat-SSeg, extending MovieChat-1K with manually annotated scene boundaries across 1,000 videos spanning movies, TV series, and documentaries.
